title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
hook: a hunter drags a snake to a grieving mother so she can watch it die, and she tells him to let it go
tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

segments.voice: Yesterday a pigeon honored the hunter who trapped his mate. Your line was the hunter laid down his nets.

After all of Bhishma's teaching, Yudhishthira is still stuck in the same place. I caused all this, he says. I'm the reason you're lying on those arrows. So when the Anushasana Parva opens, Bhishma answers with a story about blame. An old woman named Gautami finds her son dead. A snake has bitten him. A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it with a cord, and drags it to her. Tell me how to kill it, he says. Fire, or cut it to pieces? Either is fine with me.
screen: `"I CAUSED ALL THIS."` → `A BOY BITTEN BY A SNAKE.` → `"HOW SHALL I KILL IT?"`

segments.voice: Gautami says: let it go. Killing it won't bring my son back, and it won't make me any less sad. The hunter argues; surely the guilty should pay. Then the snake speaks up. Don't blame me. I didn't act on my own. Death sent me. And Death, Mrityu, appears. Don't blame me either. I was directed by Time. Then Time itself, Kala, arrives and says: none of us is the real cause. The boy's own past actions, his karma, brought him here. We were only the instruments. Gautami listens and accepts it. The hunter lets the snake go. Death and Time depart. It's a strange chain, and Bhishma means it to be. Each link points at the next, and the chain ends not in a villain but in the long working of actions and their results. Now look at who's listening. Yudhishthira is sure he's the snake, that the deaths are on him alone. Bhishma is saying, gently, that you are one link in something much longer, and you are not the whole of it. This isn't permission to stop caring. It's a way out of the kind of guilt that eats a person alive and helps nobody. And notice who sees it first. Not the warrior, not the king. A grieving old mother, with every reason to want revenge, is the one who says let it go. Anushasana means instruction, and its opening lesson, in this story, is about where blame stops.
screen: `"LET IT GO"` · `THE SNAKE, DEATH, AND TIME` · `THE CHAIN ENDS IN KARMA` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT THE WHOLE OF IT`

segments.voice: Soften your jaw and bring to mind something you still blame yourself for, and look honestly at your part in it. Then, breath by breath, let the other causes come into view, other people, timing, things nobody chose; you don't have to excuse anything, just let the picture be its true size. If you pray, you can bring that weight into your prayer.
Anushasana. Instruction: the book that opens with Gautami's story of the snake, Death and Time, and a mother who says let it go.
Your line: let it go. Tomorrow, Bhishma himself lets go. That's day eight hundred sixty-five.
